lead: A power amplifier is the last stage before the load. It must deliver watts, not millivolts, so the transistor swings over a large part of its load line. What separates one class from another is the conduction angle: the part of the input cycle during which collector current flows. Class A conducts for all 360°, class B for half of it, class C for less. Conversion efficiency rises as the conduction angle falls, and distortion rises with it. Audio systems, RF transmitters and motor drivers all pick from this menu.
prereq: You need: the DC load line, quiescent point and CE amplifier from Unit 2, Transistor Biasing and Small-Signal Amplifiers, plus the gain idea from Chapter 3.1.

sections.h3: Conduction angle, quiescent power and efficiency

blocks.text: The conduction angle is the number of degrees of the 360° input cycle for which the transistor carries collector current. Class A: 360°. Class B: 180°. Class AB: between 180° and 360°. Class C: less than 180°.
The quiescent point Q = (V_CEQ, I_CQ) is the DC operating point with no signal applied. It fixes how much power the supply hands over before any signal arrives.

blocks.where: P_out is the average AC power delivered to the load in W; P_DC is the average DC power drawn from the supply in W; η is the conversion efficiency in percent. Some syllabi call this the collector efficiency.
V_p is the peak output voltage in V and I_p the peak output current in A, for a sine wave. The factor ½ comes from averaging a sine, not from the DC values.

items: Draw the AC load line and mark Q on it.
Find the largest undistorted swing: peak voltage V_p and peak current I_p, limited by cut-off at one end and saturation at the other.
Compute P_DC = V_CC × (average current drawn from the supply).

blocks.text: Efficiency depends on drive level. At a small signal the circuit still draws nearly the same DC power but returns little AC power, so η falls far below its maximum.

In the series-fed class A stage the load resistor R_C carries the full collector current. For the largest swing, bias at the midpoint: V_CEQ = V_CC/2 and I_CQ = V_CC/(2R_C). The collector voltage can then swing up to V_CC and down to about 0 V, so the peak AC voltage is V_CC/2, and the peak AC current is I_CQ.

blocks.where: V_CC is the supply voltage in V and I_CQ the quiescent collector current in A.

blocks.text: The supply delivers V_CC continuously while the average current is I_CQ, so P_DC = V_CC I_CQ. Dividing gives η = 1/4, that is 25%.

In the transformer-coupled class A stage the primary has almost no DC resistance, so there is no DC drop across it and Q sits at V_CEQ ≈ V_CC. The collector voltage can now swing from 0 V to 2V_CC, giving a peak of V_CC, while the peak current is still I_CQ.

blocks.where: P_DC is again V_CC I_CQ in W, so the ratio doubles to one half.

blocks.text: The transformer also keeps DC out of the speaker, but it is heavy, lossy and cannot be put on a chip. Class A in any form wastes three-quarters or half of the supply power as heat, which is why it suits only low-power or high-fidelity stages.

sections.h3: Class B, class AB and class C

blocks.text: Class B conducts for 180°. Two transistors share the cycle, one for each half (the push-pull circuit is in Chapter 3.6). Each half carries a half sine, so each transistor's average current is I_p/π and the pair draws 2I_p/π.
P_out(max) = V_CC² / (2R_L) ,  P_DC = 2V_CC I_p / π ,  η = π V_p / (4 V_CC)
blocks.where: R_L is the load resistance in Ω, I_p = V_p/R_L the peak load current in A, and V_p the peak load voltage in V.

blocks.text: Put V_p = V_CC for full swing: η = π/4 = 78.5%. That is the highest efficiency any linear class can reach, because the transistor is cut off for half the cycle and burns no power then.

Class AB biases both transistors slightly on, so the conduction angle is a little over 180°, typically 200°. The small standing current removes the crossover notch. Efficiency sits between 50% and 78.5%, usually 60–70% in real audio chips.

Class C conducts for well under 180°, producing current pulses. The pulses are rich in harmonics. A tuned tank at the load filters those harmonics, so the output is nearly a sine. But class C cannot follow a changing envelope, so it is used only for constant-envelope RF signals. Efficiency can approach 85–90%, and distortion is high. RF transmitters accept that trade; audio does not. Class D switches instead of amplifying and is covered in Chapter 3.7.

figure.caption: Each row is one class: conduction angle, efficiency (typical or at full drive), and distortion. Efficiency climbs as the conduction angle shrinks; class B shows a crossover notch.

spec.title: Power amplifier classes
spec.aria: A comparison table of five amplifier classes: class A conducts 360° with 25% efficiency and low distortion; class B 180° with 78% and a crossover notch; class AB 200° with 60%; class C 120° with 85% and high distortion; class D uses PWM with 90%.

examples.question: A series-fed class A amplifier has V_CC = 12 V, R_C = 1 kΩ, and is biased exactly at midpoint so that V_CEQ = 6 V and I_CQ = 6 mA. Find the DC input power, the maximum AC output power and the conversion efficiency.
steps: Quiescent values: V_CEQ = 6 V, I_CQ = 6 mA. Check: I_CQ = V_CC/(2R_C) = 12/(2 × 1 kΩ) = 6 mA, so the bias is indeed at midpoint.
DC power: P_DC = V_CC × I_CQ = 12 V × 6 mA = 72 mW.
Largest swing: the collector voltage can rise to 12 V and fall to 0 V, so the peak AC voltage is V_p = 6 V. Cut-off limits the peak current to I_p = 6 mA.
AC output: P_out(max) = (V_p × I_p)/2 = (6 V × 6 mA)/2 = 18 mW.
examples.answer: P_DC = 72 mW, P_out(max) = 18 mW, and η = 25%, which is exactly the series-fed class A limit.
examples.check:
Vcc = 12.0
Ic = 6e-3
Vp = 6.0
Ip = 6e-3
Pdc = Vcc * Ic
Pout = Vp * Ip / 2
eta = 100 * Pout / Pdc
print(round(Pdc * 1000, 2))
print(round(Pout * 1000, 2))
print(round(eta, 2))

examples.question: A push-pull class B stage runs from V_CC = 12 V into an 8 Ω loudspeaker and is driven to full swing. Find the peak load current, the maximum output power, the DC power drawn and the efficiency.
steps: Peak load current: I_p = V_CC / R_L = 12 V / 8 Ω = 1.5 A.
Maximum output power: P_out = V_CC × I_p / 2 = 12 V × 1.5 A / 2 = 9 W.
DC power: P_DC = 2 V_CC I_p / π = (2 × 12 V × 1.5 A) / π = 11.46 W.
Efficiency: η = 9 W / 11.46 W = 0.785 = 78.5%, which is π/4.
examples.answer: P_out(max) = 9 W, P_DC = 11.46 W, η = 78.5%, the class B ceiling.
examples.check:
import math
Vcc = 12.0
RL = 8.0
Ip = Vcc / RL
Pout = Vcc * Ip / 2
Pdc = 2 * Vcc * Ip / math.pi
eta = 100 * Pout / Pdc
print(round(Ip, 2))
print(round(Pout, 2))
print(round(Pdc, 2))
print(round(eta, 1))

traps: Dropping the factor ½ and writing P_out = V_p × I_p. That doubles the answer and can push efficiency past 100%.
Treating V_CC × I_CQ as AC power. It is the DC input power; the AC output is always smaller.
Mixing the two class A limits: series-fed gives 25%, transformer-coupled gives 50%. Write which circuit you mean before quoting a number.
Quoting 78.5% for class B at any drive. The formula η = πV_p/(4V_CC) falls with swing; 78.5% holds only at V_p = V_CC.
Saying class AB removes distortion. It removes the crossover notch only; clipping and harmonic distortion remain (see Chapter 3.8).

quiz.q: Define conduction angle. Give its value for class A, class B and class C.
quiz.a: The conduction angle is the part of the 360° input cycle for which collector current flows. Class A: 360°. Class B: 180°. Class C: less than 180°.

quiz.q: State the maximum conversion efficiency of series-fed class A, transformer-coupled class A and class B.
quiz.a: 25% for series-fed class A, 50% for transformer-coupled class A, 78.5% (π/4) for class B at full swing.

quiz.q: Why does the transformer-coupled class A stage reach 50% while the series-fed stage reaches only 25%?
quiz.a: The transformer primary has almost no DC resistance, so Q sits near V_CC instead of V_CC/2. The collector can swing from 0 V to 2V_CC, doubling the peak AC voltage for the same DC power V_CC I_CQ. P_out doubles from V_CC I_CQ/4 to V_CC I_CQ/2, so η doubles from 25% to 50%.

quiz.q: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier has V_CC = 10 V and I_CQ = 100 mA. Find P_DC, P_out(max) and η.
quiz.a: P_DC = 10 V × 0.1 A = 1 W. Peak swing is V_CC = 10 V at I_p = 0.1 A, so P_out = (10 × 0.1)/2 = 0.5 W. η = 0.5/1 = 50%.

quiz.q: A push-pull class B stage with V_CC = 20 V drives R_L = 16 Ω at full swing. Find I_p, P_out, P_DC and η.
For a class B stage, at what fraction of full output swing does the efficiency equal 50%?
quiz.a: η = πV_p/(4V_CC) = 0.5 gives V_p = 2V_CC/π = 0.637V_CC. So η is only 50% at about 64% of the maximum peak voltage, even though P_out is already at (0.637)² ≈ 40% of its maximum. Low drive means poor efficiency.

quiz.q: A class A stage is biased at midpoint. Explain why its efficiency at half the maximum swing is far below 25%.
quiz.a: P_DC = V_CC I_CQ stays fixed because the average current hardly changes with signal. Halving the peak voltage quarters P_out to one quarter of its maximum (25%/4), so η falls to about 6%.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real audio chips are class AB or class D, and class D now dominates portable speakers and car audio. RF designers use class E and class F, which shape the drain voltage and current waveforms so they barely overlap, pushing efficiency past 80% at gigahertz frequencies. 5G base stations add envelope tracking, which moves the supply voltage up and down with the signal so the amplifier stays near saturation. Gallium nitride transistors, with high breakdown voltage and low loss, are the current choice for such stages. Search next: class E amplifier, class F amplifier, Doherty amplifier, envelope tracking, GaN HEMT power amplifier.
